intro: Houston does not do walks, and neither does this page. The city sprawls across seventeen hundred square kilometres and its oldest trees are scattered accordingly: a live oak with a forty metre crown in Spring Branch, the tallest winged elm in Texas, a pecan with a footpath named after it, a live oak in Klein a gas station nearly took down, a yaupon in a museum garden, a wide oak in Bellaire, and two old live oaks downtown. Eight trees, each worth the trip.
meta_description: Eleven remarkable trees around Houston: a live oak with a 40 metre crown, the tallest winged elm in Texas, and two old live oaks downtown.
question_meta: Houston's oldest tree is the Kissing Tree at Klein, a live oak that marks an 1848 homestead. Where it stands, and ten more worth the trip.
question_answer: The oldest tree around Houston is almost certainly the Kissing Tree at Klein, a live oak that Strack family records place at the site of Herman Strack's homestead and blacksmith shop, settled in 1848, and which was already the meeting tree for the settlement then. Nobody has put a firm number of years on it. The largest is a different tree: a live oak on the lawn of John Knox Presbyterian Church in Spring Branch, measured in March 2026 at 625 centimetres round and twenty three metres tall, with a crown spreading forty metres. Neither is in central Houston. Downtown has two old live oaks, Jane Ellen's Tree in Sam Houston Park and the Old Hanging Oak on Capitol Street, credited with 250 to 400 years, but those ages are estimates that nobody has measured.
question_context: Measurements here come from the Texas Big Tree Registry, kept by the Texas A&M Forest Service, which records circumference, height and crown spread with the date each was taken. That is unusually good for a tree register, which is why the girths on this page are exact and the ages are not: the registry has no age field at all, and nobody has cored these trees. Where a year appears it comes from a settlement date or a plaque rather than from the wood. The registry publishes in inches and feet, and the figures here are converted. It also marks which of its trees stand on public land and which do not, and withholds the positions of the private ones, so several large Houston trees are deliberately absent from this page. The two downtown oaks are not registry trees: their ages and pins come from the Heritage Society and the press, and both pins are approximate. The one thing the registry is good at, and most registers are not, is telling you a tree was alive recently: three of these trees were measured in the last twelve months.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Houston?
faq.a: Probably the Kissing Tree at Klein, north of the city, which marks the site of Herman Strack's 1848 homestead and was the settlement's gathering tree. No firm age has been published for it. The biggest is the live oak at John Knox Presbyterian Church in Spring Branch, 625 centimetres round when it was measured in March 2026.

faq.q: Are any of these in central Houston?
faq.a: Two, and both are estimates. Jane Ellen's Tree stands in Sam Houston Park and the Old Hanging Oak on the corner of Capitol and Bagby, about half a kilometre apart. Their ages come from the Heritage Society and press reports rather than any measurement, and our pins mark the park and the corner, not the trunk. The other trees are further out: the nearest is the Spring Branch live oak, about eighteen kilometres west of downtown. The two registry trees closest to downtown stand on private land, and the registry withholds their positions.

faq.q: How do you know these trees are still alive?
faq.a: Because they were measured recently and the registry records the date. The Spring Branch live oak and the Sugar Land pecan were measured in March 2026 and the winged elm in December 2025. That is a better answer than most tree registers can give, since almost none of them carry a vitality field at all.

faq.q: Why is a tree of 279 centimetres on a list with one of 625?
faq.a: Because it is the state champion winged elm, and champion status is scored on trunk, height and crown together rather than girth alone. At thirty metres it is a tall tree for its species, and there is no larger winged elm recorded in Texas.

trees.name: The John Knox Live Oak

location.address: John Knox Presbyterian Church, 2525 Gessner Road

trees.story:
The crown is the thing. Forty metres across, on a trunk 625 centimetres round and a tree only twenty three metres tall, which is the live oak habit taken to its conclusion: this species does not race upward, it spreads until the branches come back down to meet you. The Texas A&M Forest Service measured it in March 2026, so those are current numbers rather than remembered ones.

It stands on the front lawn of a Presbyterian church on Gessner Road, in a part of Spring Branch that was farmland when the congregation broke ground in 1961. The church's own history mentions picnics held under the big trees at the front of the property, which is roughly what a tree this shape is for.

No age has been published. Live oaks are difficult to date without coring and nobody appears to have done it. What can be said is that a live oak reaching six metres of girth in a climate like this one has had a long time and a lot of water, and that it was clearly here before the church was.

The grounds are open, and a churchyard has never been a bad place to stand and look up.
verified_sources: https://texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry (Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service, measured March 2026)
trees.access: Free. Church grounds, open. The tree stands on the front lawn, visible from Gessner Road.
trees.transport: About 18 km west of downtown Houston. Drive; there is parking on site.
trees.how_to_recognise: A low, enormously wide live oak on an open church lawn, far broader than it is tall, with limbs reaching almost to the grass.

trees.name: The Old Pecan Tree

location.address: Old Pecan Tree Trail, Sugar Land

trees.story:
There is a footpath in Sugar Land called Old Pecan Tree Trail, and it is named after exactly what you would hope. The tree is a pecan of 467 centimetres round and twenty eight metres tall, with a crown spreading twenty five metres, measured by the Texas A&M Forest Service in March 2026. Trail guides rank it among the twenty five largest trees in Texas, which is scored on trunk, height and crown together.

Pecan is the state tree, and it is one of the few state trees anywhere chosen for something other than looks: it feeds people. A tree this size drops a serious crop, and in a good year the ground beneath it is worth walking slowly across in October.

The trail is short, well under a kilometre, and the tree is the reason it exists. That is the useful thing about a path named for a tree: nobody has to explain where to go.

No age has been recorded. Pecans of this girth in the Brazos bottomlands are generally reckoned in centuries rather than decades, but nobody has counted the rings and this page is not going to guess.
verified_sources: https://texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry (Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service, measured March 2026)
trees.access: Free. Public hiking trail, open daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 32 km southwest of downtown Houston, in Sugar Land. Drive.
trees.how_to_recognise: A tall, straight-trunked pecan standing well clear of the trees around it, on the short trail that carries its name.

best_time.label: October, when the nuts come down

trees.name: The Kissing Tree
trees.age_estimate: already the settlement's meeting tree in 1848

location.address: Behind the Circle K at Stuebner Airline Road, Klein

trees.story:
Herman Strack landed at Galveston in 1848, a blacksmith out of Prussia and the first of five brothers to settle north Harris County. Family records put his homestead and forge at this tree. It got its name from what happened under it afterwards: couples met here, and a good number of proposals were made in its shade.

Everything else the Stracks built is gone. When the family restaurant closed in 2014 a developer bought the land for a Circle K, and the tree stood where the forecourt entrance needed to be. That was very nearly the end of it. Students at Klein Oaks High School ran a letter-writing campaign, Circle K eventually pledged to keep the tree, and three years later the Texas A&M Forest Service made it a Famous Tree of Texas.

So it is a live oak hung with Spanish moss on a patch of grass behind a filling station, and it is the last physical trace of a settlement that gave the whole district its name. Nobody has dated it. It was already the tree everyone met at in 1848, which puts a floor under the number if not a ceiling.
verified_sources: https://famoustreesoftexas.tfs.tamu.edu/ (Texas A&M Forest Service, Famous Trees of Texas)
trees.access: Free. Public access, on open ground behind a filling station.
trees.transport: About 33 km north of downtown Houston, at Klein. Drive.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad live oak draped in Spanish moss, standing alone on a grass patch behind a Circle K forecourt.

trees.name: The Spring Creek Winged Elm

location.address: Spring Creek Greenway Trail, Harris County Precinct 4

trees.story:
This is the largest winged elm recorded in Texas, and it is not a large tree. The trunk is 279 centimetres round, which for the species is remarkable and for this page is modest. Champion status is scored on trunk, height and crown added together, and where this tree wins is height: thirty metres, which is tall for an elm that usually tops out well short of that, with a twenty four metre crown above it.

Winged elm gets its name from the corky ridges that run down either side of the younger twigs, wide enough to look deliberate. On a tree this old you will find them out at the ends of the branches rather than on the trunk, so it is worth picking up a fallen twig.

It stands on the Spring Creek Greenway, a long ribbon of bottomland forest that Harris County has been stitching together along the creek for years, and which is one of the largest urban forested corridors in the country. The Forest Service measured the tree in December 2025.

No age is recorded. Winged elm is not a long-lived species, so this one is old for its kind rather than old in the way an oak is old.
verified_sources: https://texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry (Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service, state champion, measured December 2025)
trees.access: Free. Public county greenway trail, open daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 31 km north of downtown Houston. Drive to a greenway trailhead.
trees.how_to_recognise: A notably tall, slender elm in bottomland forest beside Spring Creek, with corky ridges running along the younger twigs.

trees.name: The Rienzi Yaupon
verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service, TreeID 1128 (state champion class, circumference 36 in / 91 cm, spread 28.5 ft, height 31 ft, condition code 3, owner of record Rienzi/Museum of Fine Arts Houston, PublicOrPrivate=1, Display=1, MEASURED AUGUST 2024, one of the most recently re-measured trees in this batch)

Houston Chronicle's Azalea Trail coverage of Rienzi's gardens, independently describing yaupons as part of the garden's evergreen structure at this site; mfah.org's own Rienzi visiting-hours page confirms the four-acre garden is free and open for self-guided visits daily except Sundays before 1pm and the whole month of August
trees.access: Free. Rienzi's gardens are open for self-guided walking every day, Mon-Sat 10am-4:30pm and Sun 1-4:30pm, no ticket or reservation needed for the garden itself (only the house tour is reservation-based). Closed the entire month of August.
trees.transport: In central Houston (River Oaks), roughly 5 km from downtown; walkable from nearby Kirby Dr bus stops.
trees.story:
Texas keeps a champion register for its biggest trees, and this entry is a plant most of the South clips into a hedge. Yaupon holly usually grows as a dense evergreen shrub. The one in the gardens at Rienzi has gone up like a tree: just over nine metres tall, a crown spreading nearly as wide, and a trunk 91 centimetres round, which is enough for state champion class on the Texas A&M Forest Service's registry. Foresters taped it in August 2024, which makes it one of the freshest measurements on this map.

The four acres it grows in belong to the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. The Houston Chronicle's Azalea Trail coverage describes the garden's yaupons as part of its evergreen structure, the quiet green that holds the place together while everything else takes its turn flowering. Walking the garden costs nothing and needs no reservation, though the whole property shuts for the month of August.

Two things we cannot tell you. Only the state registry names this particular plant, so it sits flagged here until a second source catches up with it. And nobody has dated it: yaupon gets measured for girth far more often than for years, and no growth rate we would trust for the species turned up. If you know how long it has been standing there, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the size for the species: a yaupon holly grown to tree height, just over nine metres on a trunk 91 centimetres round. It stands in Rienzi's four-acre garden off Kirby Drive.

trees.name: The Russ Pitman Mexican White Oak

location.address: Russ Pitman Park / Nature Discovery Center, 7112 Newcastle St, Bellaire, TX 77401

verified_sources: Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service, TreeID 2359 (circumference 91 in / 231 cm, spread 65 ft, height 62 ft, condition code 2, owner of record Nature Discovery Center, PublicOrPrivate=1, Display=1, measured May 2020)

naturediscoverycenter.org and bellairetx.gov both independently confirm Russ Pitman Park is a City of Bellaire public park (open 5am-9:30pm daily, free) that hosts the Nature Discovery Center, and describe the park's 'towering oak trees'; the registry's owner field (Nature Discovery Center) matches this site exactly
trees.access: Free. Russ Pitman Park is a City of Bellaire public park, open 5am to 9:30pm every day; the Nature Discovery Center building itself keeps separate, more limited hours, but the park and its trees are open on the park's own hours.
trees.transport: In Bellaire, inside the West Loop (610); roughly 10 km from downtown Houston, drive or bus.
trees.story:
This oak is broader than it is tall. The Texas A&M Forest Service put its crown at 19.8 metres across against 18.9 metres of height, taped the trunk at 2.31 metres round, and rated its condition good.

It grows in Russ Pitman Park in Bellaire, a separate city sitting inside Houston's West Loop. Both the park's own pages and the City of Bellaire's describe the place by its towering oaks, in the plural, without picking one out. The state registry did pick one out, and this is it: a Mexican white oak, Quercus polymorpha, also known as the Monterrey oak, which is not the species you expect to find carrying a state measurement in a Texas suburb.

The park is public and free, open from five in the morning until half past nine at night, with the Nature Discovery Center inside it keeping its own shorter hours. The tree is reachable whenever the park is, which is most of the day.

Two gaps worth saying out loud. The registry's tape went round it in May 2020, so the figures above are five years old and read as a floor rather than a reading; nothing we found suggests it has come down or gone into decline. And no age exists for it anywhere, with no growth rate for this species we would trust to derive one from the girth. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, wider than the tree is tall at 19.8 metres across, on a trunk 2.31 metres round. It stands among the oaks of Russ Pitman Park, off Newcastle Street in Bellaire.

trees.name: Jane Ellen's Tree

location.address: Sam Houston Park, 1000 Bagby St, Houston, TX 77002

trees.access: Free; Sam Houston Park is a public downtown park (owner-managed by the Heritage Society).
trees.transport: Downtown Houston, METRORail Main Street line to Preston or Downtown Transit Center, about 10 to 15 min walk to the park.
trees.story:
Houston is younger than this tree, probably by the better part of a century. The Heritage Society, which manages Sam Houston Park, puts the oak at 250 to 300 years old. That is an arborist's estimate rather than a ring count, and nobody has published a girth to check it against, but even the low end has it growing here before the city was founded in 1836.

It is a southern live oak grown the way the species grows when it is left alone: sprawling rather than tall, with massive limbs that reach out and then down until they nearly meet the ground. The towers of downtown stand a few blocks away. The oak was already old when the frontier town became a cotton port, and older still when the oil money arrived and built the skyline behind it.

The name is recent. The society called it Jane Ellen's Tree, after Jane Ellen, its first female executive director, so it honours the person who looked after the ground rather than anyone who owned it.

Do not confuse it with the other live oak that made the news in this park. In February 2026 Trees for Houston planted its one-millionth tree here, a young live oak beside the Kellum-Noble House. It has a long future ahead of it. This one has the past.

Our pin marks the park, not the trunk, so expect to look around. Look for the limbs that come down to meet you.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its massive limbs, sprawling outward and reaching down almost to the ground. It stands in Sam Houston Park; the young live oak beside the Kellum-Noble House, planted in 2026, is not it.

trees.name: The Old Hanging Oak

location.address: Corner of Capitol St and Bagby St, across from Bayou Place, Downtown Houston, TX

verified_sources: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/old-hanging-oak (seen only as a search snippet, page 403; lead not source)
trees.access: Free; on the public sidewalk area at the corner, maintained by the City of Houston Civic Center Department.
trees.transport: Downtown, next to Bayou Place; METRORail Main Street line stops about 5 to 8 min walk away.
trees.story:
The most famous thing about this oak is a story nobody can document. For years a plaque near the corner of Capitol and Bagby said that eleven criminals were hanged from its limbs while Texas was an independent republic, between 1836 and 1845. The plaque has since gone, and the story has not held up well without it. The Houston Press calls it uncertain. The Houston Chronicle has called the tree's grim reputation false. And the executions that a 1913 history of the city by Dr S.O. Young does record, three of them according to the Press, are tied to a different tree altogether, in Freedmans Town.

What remains is the oak itself, which is the better story anyway. It is a southern live oak usually described as roughly 400 years old. Nobody has published a ring count or even a girth, so treat that as a figure the city repeats rather than one anybody measured. It is old; exactly how old is an open question.

It has stood through all of downtown Houston's history without the courtesy of a park around it. It stands on the public sidewalk across the street from Bayou Place, and the City of Houston's Civic Center Department keeps it alive there.

Our pin is an estimate of the corner, not the trunk, so check which tree you are looking at. And if you have a tape measure, the girth would settle more than the plaque ever did.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old live oak on the corner of Capitol Street and Bagby Street. It stands on the public sidewalk, across the street from Bayou Place.

trees.name: The Becks Prime Augusta Live Oaks

location.address: Becks Prime, 2615 Augusta Dr, Houston, TX 77057 (behind the restaurant)

trees.access: Visible from the patio and the drive-through lane of a counter-service restaurant, listed as open daily from 11am to 10pm in 2026. These are a business's grounds rather than a park, so come during opening hours.
trees.transport: Car or bus along the Westheimer Rd corridor near the Galleria; no rail; walk time not verified
trees.story:
Most restaurants buy land for the parking. The owners of this Becks Prime bought theirs in 1988, by a local news account, mainly for the trees. Two live oaks stand behind the building on Augusta Drive, each reported at about 70 feet tall, and the Heritage Society, Houston's history museum, estimates the oak it names at 400 to 500 years old. Another account has them sprouting around the 1620s. Neither figure comes with a ring count or a girth, so read both as estimates. Even the low end has these oaks standing well before Houston was founded in 1836.

What makes them worth the detour is what the restaurant did around them. Their lower limbs had sunk until they rested on the ground, so a 210-ton crane lifted them back up onto wooden stilts, which still hold them today. The building is said to float 18 inches above the soil to keep its weight off the roots, and the drive-through lane that runs under the canopy is laid in pavers set by hand.

The sources do not agree on the count. The Heritage Society speaks of one oak, the local report of two colossal ones. Stand on the patio and count for yourself.

These are a business's grounds, not a park, so come while the restaurant is open. Our pin marks the address rather than the trunks.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the limbs propped up on wooden stilts, with the drive-through lane running under the canopy. They stand behind the Becks Prime restaurant at 2615 Augusta Drive.

trees.name: The Cemetery Oak

location.address: Glenwood Cemetery, 2525 Washington Ave, Houston, TX 77007 (in the back of the cemetery, halfway up the slope)

trees.access: Free; the cemetery is open daily, 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. It is a working cemetery with its own rules, and photography is restricted unless the cemetery has authorised it, so check those rules before you take pictures.
trees.transport: Washington Ave corridor; METRO bus along Washington Ave; walk time from a stop not verified
trees.story:
The puzzle of this oak is where it stands: in a narrow walkway between graves, halfway up a slope at the back of Glenwood Cemetery. Planting a live oak in a path that skinny would be an odd choice, which is why historians quoted by the Houston Chronicle in 2010 suspected the tree was here first, growing on its own before anyone was buried around it. If they are right, every grave in that row arrived after the oak did.

Glenwood itself calls it perhaps its most notable tree, aptly named The Cemetery Oak, and that is saying something. The same grounds hold two Harris County champion trees, a mockernut hickory on East Avenue and an eastern red cedar in Section C-3, and the cemetery still puts the oak above both.

Its age is an estimate. In the Chronicle's account a landscape architect put it at about 130 years, judging from its size and from a 1930 aerial photograph, which would start it around 1880. A 2013 photo caption says only well over a hundred years. Take a century to two as the honest band. The same piece described the trunk as wide as a Volkswagen, but nobody has published a tape measurement we could check.

Our pin marks the cemetery, not the tree, and the grounds cover 88 acres. Head for the back and look halfway up the slope. If you measure the girth, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, once described as wide as a Volkswagen, rising from a narrow walkway between graves. It stands at the back of Glenwood Cemetery, halfway up the slope.

trees.name: The Ravine Trail Sycamore

location.address: Ravine Trail, northwest corner of the Houston Arboretum & Nature Center, 4501 Woodway Dr, Houston, TX 77024

trees.access: Free admission, parking $6.50 (free Thursdays and the second Sunday of each month); grounds and trails open 7 am to 7:30 pm daily (owner's site). Seen from the Ravine Trail boardwalk.
trees.transport: Car; Woodway Dr entrance; transit and walk times not verified
trees.story:
The claim attached to this sycamore is a rumour, and we are keeping it one. Houstonia magazine's 2022 guide to the Houston Arboretum and Nature Center describes a leviathan sycamore on the Ravine Trail, rumored to be the oldest of its species in Harris County. Rumored is the magazine's word, and it is ours too. We have found no register entry, no measurement and no ring count behind it, and the arboretum's own trail pages do not mention this tree at all.

What is not in doubt is where to look. The Ravine Trail runs through the northwest corner of the arboretum, crossing a water-filled ravine on a series of bridges, and the big trees along it are seen from the boardwalk. The arboretum is free to enter, so the only cost of checking the rumour for yourself is the parking.

One caution before you decide you have found it. The arboretum's own pages say sycamores also grow tall on the Couch Birding Trail, so a big sycamore elsewhere in the grounds is not necessarily this one. The one the magazine meant is on the Ravine Trail.

Nobody has published its age, its girth or its height. If you go with a tape measure, take the trunk's circumference at chest height and tell us; it is the quickest way to find out whether the rumour stands up. Our pin marks the arboretum entrance, not the tree, and the ravine may be several hundred metres from it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big sycamore seen from the boardwalk on the Ravine Trail, by the bridges over the water-filled ravine. It stands in the northwest corner of the arboretum, not on the Couch Birding Trail.
